baseline: Host Linux 6.8: timer_create01 reports passed 40, failed 0. It calls raw __NR_timer_create for 5 sigev_notify values (SIGEV_NONE=1, SIGEV_SIGNAL=0, SIGEV_THREAD=2, SIGEV_THREAD_ID=4, and a NULL sigevent) across 8 clocks, then timer_delete()s each. Per assertion, the correct kernel returns 0 and writes a timer id for every notify type, including SIGEV_THREAD. Confirmed directly with a raw-syscall probe that bypasses glibc: notify=0/1/2/4 all return 0, while notify=3 and 5 return EINVAL. A SIGEV_THREAD timer armed via timer_settime then delivered SIGALRM with si_code=-2 (SI_TIMER), i.e. the kernel treats SIGEV_THREAD exactly as SIGEV_SIGNAL and enqueues to the thread group; it never spawns a thread. Thread creation for SIGEV_THREAD is entirely glibc userspace emulation (glibc converts it to SIGEV_THREAD_ID aimed at its own helper thread and never passes SIGEV_THREAD to the kernel). Signo validation is also identical for SIGEV_SIGNAL and SIGEV_THREAD: signo in 1..=SIGRTMAX(64) accepted, 0 / 65 / -1 rejected with EINVAL, whereas SIGEV_NONE ignores signo entirely.
failing_assertion: No assertion is reached. Asterinas panics inside the syscall before the test produces any output: 'Uncaught panic: not implemented at kernel/src/syscall/timer_create.rs:74'. Expected sys_timer_create(CLOCK_*, {sigev_notify=SIGEV_THREAD}, &id) = 0; actual = kernel panic. Because PANIC_ON_OOPS defaults to true, the panic handler takes the 'Halt the system' path and calls panic::abort(), so the whole kernel dies rather than just the thread. The LTP runner buffers into $LOG_FILE and only cat's it after kirk exits (run_ltp_test.sh line 34), so the halt discards every result from that boot, not just this test's.
root_cause: In sys_timer_create (kernel/src/syscall/timer_create.rs), sigev_notify is parsed into SigNotify at line 55 and dispatched by a match at lines 57-96 that builds the timer's expiry closure. SIGEV_NONE (59), SIGEV_SIGNAL (61-67) and SIGEV_THREAD_ID (77-95) each construct a closure, but the SIGEV_THREAD arm at lines 73-75 is a bare `unimplemented!()` with a TODO saying the system cannot yet spawn a POSIX thread to run sigev_un._sigev_thread.function. SIGEV_THREAD = 2 is a fully valid value that SigNotify::try_from accepts, so the match arm is reachable with well-formed input: any unprivileged process passing sigev_notify=SIGEV_THREAD executes the `unimplemented!()`, which is a Rust panic. The TODO's premise is wrong about what the syscall owes the caller -- Linux's kernel also does not spawn any thread for SIGEV_THREAD; it validates signo and enqueues the signal to the thread group exactly as for SIGEV_SIGNAL, and the callback thread is glibc's job. So the missing capability the TODO waits on is not actually required, and the arm can be satisfied with the same signal-enqueue logic already present two arms above it.
invariant: A syscall must never panic on well-formed, in-range arguments from unprivileged userspace; an unimplemented but valid input must be reported as an errno to the caller, never as a kernel oops. Specifically for timer_create: sigev_notify=SIGEV_THREAD is a valid notification type that the kernel satisfies by queueing sigev_signo to the calling process's thread group on expiry (spawning the notification thread is a libc responsibility, not the kernel's), and sigev_signo must be validated in 1..=SIGRTMAX for every notify type that delivers a signal.
owning_layer: The syscall entry layer -- the sigevent interpretation in sys_timer_create (kernel/src/syscall/timer_create.rs). This is where sigev_notify is validated and translated into an expiry action, and it is the layer that owes userspace an errno rather than a panic. Asterinas has no separate posix-timer core layer between the syscall and the per-clock TimerManager, so unlike Linux (which splits do_timer_create/good_sigevent from the k_itimer core) the syscall entry function is the closest equivalent to Linux's good_sigevent placement, and it is the correct home for this rule. Note the narrowest possible edit is the single match arm at lines 73-75, but the invariant belongs to this whole dispatch: the sibling `unimplemented!()` arms in the same file's create_timer helper (lines 158, 169, 172) violate the same rule and are reachable from userspace on a negative clockid, including via sys_timerfd_create, which passes clockid through unvalidated.
linux_reference: Linux enforces this in the syscall entry path for posix timers: kernel/time/posix-timers.c, do_timer_create() delegates sigevent checking to good_sigevent(), which switches on sigev_notify and treats SIGEV_SIGNAL and SIGEV_THREAD identically -- both validate sigev_signo via valid_signal() and target the thread group -- while only SIGEV_THREAD_ID looks up a specific task, and anything else returns NULL so the syscall returns -EINVAL. No arm can panic the kernel. Direct web reads of elixir.bootlin.com and man7.org were blocked from this container, so this placement is asserted from the raw-syscall probe results rather than from reading the source text: the probe reproduces exactly good_sigevent's observable contract (notify 0/1/2/4 accepted and 3/5 rejected; signo validated for 0/2/4 but not for 1; SIGEV_THREAD expiry delivering SI_TIMER to the process). The behavioural evidence is solid; the file/function attribution is from prior knowledge and unverified in this run.
other_callers: For the line-74 panic specifically, nobody else: sys_timer_create is the only caller that parses a sigevent. sys_timerfd_create reaches the shared create_timer helper (kernel/src/time/timerfd.rs:106) but supplies its own expiry closure and never touches sigev_notify, so it cannot hit line 74. That makes a one-arm fix defensible. The broader invariant does have a second caller though: the dynamic-clock `unimplemented!()` arms in create_timer (lines 158, 169, 172) are reachable from both sys_timer_create and sys_timerfd_create by passing a negative clockid that decodes to a SCHED or FD dynamic clock, since sys_timerfd_create (kernel/src/syscall/timerfd_create.rs:17) forwards clockid without validation. Those are the same class of userspace-triggerable kernel halt and are worth noting even if out of scope for this test.
suggested_direction: Replace the `unimplemented!()` at kernel/src/syscall/timer_create.rs:73-75 with the same signal-enqueue action used by the SIGEV_SIGNAL arm: validate sigev_signo through SigNum::try_from and return a closure that calls current_process.enqueue_signal(KernelSignal::new(signo)), so SIGEV_THREAD behaves as Linux does. Update the stale TODO to record that the kernel deliberately treats SIGEV_THREAD as SIGEV_SIGNAL and that spawning the notification thread is libc's responsibility, so no future thread-spawning API is needed here. A probe patch doing exactly this was applied, booted, and then reverted: the test went from a kernel halt with zero output to passed 25 / skipped 15 / failed 0 / broken 0, where the 25 are the 5 supported clocks (CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID, CLOCK_BOOTTIME) across all 5 notify types, and the 15 skipped are CLOCK_BOOTTIME_ALARM(8), CLOCK_REALTIME_ALARM(9) and CLOCK_TAI(11), which are absent from Asterinas's ClockId enum (kernel/src/syscall/clock_gettime.rs:41-50, stops at CLOCK_BOOTTIME=7) and so return EINVAL, which the test maps to TCONF via possibly_unsupported(). The runner requires failed/broken/warnings to be 0 but permits skipped, so this one-arm change is sufficient to turn the test green; adding the alarm/TAI clocks is a separate missing-feature and is not needed. Consider also converting the sibling dynamic-clock `unimplemented!()` arms to EINVAL/ENOTSUP returns to close the same defect class, and note the pre-existing `signo as u8` truncation in the SIGEV_SIGNAL and SIGEV_THREAD_ID arms (sigev_signo=257 truncates to 1 and is wrongly accepted where Linux returns EINVAL) as a related but independent bug.
